title: An Indian Writer Just Won One of the Commonwealth's Most Coveted Literary Prizes — With a Story About Mehendi
excerpt: Sharon Aruparayil's 'Mehendi Nights' beat 7,806 entries from 54 countries to take the Asia regional prize, placing her one step from the £5,000 global crown
body:
The 2026 Commonwealth Short Story Prize, one of the English-speaking world's most prestigious awards for unpublished fiction, has announced its five regional winners — and the Asia prize belongs to **Sharon Aruparayil**, an Indian writer whose story *Mehendi Nights* navigates the harsh textures of a girl's life through the lens of henna ritual, societal oppression and the quiet defiance of art.

Published by **Granta**, the story was selected from 7,806 entries submitted across 54 Commonwealth nations. Aruparayil now advances to the final round; the overall winner, who takes home **£5,000** (approximately ₹5.4 lakh), will be announced in late June 2026. Each regional winner receives **£2,500**.

## What the Story Is About

*Mehendi Nights* traces the inner world of a young girl living in a polluted city, caught between her *aai*'s expectations and the oppressive weight of the society around her. The narrative centres on a mehendi ceremony — that most familiar of Indian rituals — and transforms it into a site of resistance. Through the symbolic power of henna patterns, the protagonist finds a language that circumvents the constraints imposed on her, making art both an escape and a confrontation.

It is a story that will resonate with anyone who grew up in an Indian household where rituals carried meanings that were never fully explained — and where the women who performed them were never fully seen.

## India's Quiet Dominance in the Prize

Aruparayil is the latest in a striking run of Indian and Indian-origin winners at the Commonwealth Short Story Prize. In 2024, Mumbai writer **Sanjana Thakur** won the overall global prize with *Aishwarya Rai*, a story that satirised Bollywood beauty standards and explored motherhood and identity. That win followed years of strong Indian representation on the shortlist.

This year, three Indian writers made the Asia shortlist: Aruparayil for *Mehendi Nights*, **Rafaa Dalvi** for *Thirty-One Steps*, and **Rupsa Dey** for *Fighting Elsewhere*. The Asia region also featured shortlisted writers from Bangladesh, Singapore and Malaysia — but it was Aruparayil's work that the judges singled out for its layered examination of power and resilience.

The broader 2026 shortlist of 25 writers from 14 countries included **John Edward DeMicoli**, who became the first Maltese writer ever shortlisted, and returning entrants from Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana and Nigeria. The judging panel included South African journalist and author **Fred Khumalo**, alongside judges from Bangladesh, Canada, Jamaica and Australia.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For NRI readers — many of whom grew up watching their mothers and grandmothers apply mehendi before weddings and festivals — Aruparayil's subject matter is intimately recognisable. But the story's real power lies in its refusal to treat Indian ritual as decorative or nostalgic. *Mehendi Nights* insists that the patterns pressed into skin carry political weight, that beauty and oppression are not opposites but neighbours.

Indian writing in English has long been dominated by a handful of familiar names — the Rushdies, the Roys, the Lahiris. Prizes like the Commonwealth Short Story Prize matter because they surface writers who are not yet part of that canon but whose work speaks with equal force. Aruparayil's win is a reminder that the most powerful Indian stories are often the quietest.

## What's Next

All shortlisted stories will be published on **adda**, the Commonwealth Foundation's online literary magazine. The overall winner will be announced at the Commonwealth Short Story Prize ceremony in late June 2026. If Aruparayil takes the global prize, she will join Thakur in giving India back-to-back wins — a feat no country has achieved in the prize's 14-year history.
